WA-SC was characterized by widespread synergy, while WA-CS and WA-HQ showed stronger trade-off tendencies in the semi-arid zone. The WA-FP relationship was generally weak. Path analysis indicated that climate factors exerted significant direct effects on WA-ES trade-offs, whereas synergies were jointly regulated by topography, soil, human activities, and habitat quality. title: Combining detection dogs with air extraction methodology to expose wildlife trafficking in containerized cargo

title: Endangered species laws and the inclusion of Indigenous knowledges and sciences in risk assessments

title: Centering geospatial data uncertainty and the potential for injustice in pastoralist rangeland conservation prioritization
authors: Ryan R. Unks
abstract: Procedural, distributional, recognitional, and epistemic justice aspects of conservation interventions are well documented in contexts where pastoralism is a key livelihood and way of life. When they are used to provide evidence for conservation interventions, the inherent uncertainties and limitations of geospatial data and analyses, coupled with ongoing political marginalization of pastoralists, creates a high risk of perpetuating historical injustices and extending new injustices. title: Extrapolation strategy matters when transferring ecological niche models: new visualization tools for informed decisions

abstract: Abstract Ecological niche models (ENMs) are commonly used to predict species' potential distributions across space and time, allowing researchers and practitioners to assess invasion risk, estimate the impacts of future climate change, and reconstruct past distributions. These predictions, however, often require extrapolation into environmental conditions that fall outside the range of values used for model training (i.e. ‘non‐analog environments'). Two primary strategies exist for extrapolating into new conditions for some modeling algorithms: unconstrained extrapolation (allowing the modeled response curve to maintain its trajectory) and clamping (holding the response constant at the values observed at the limits of the training data). As these can lead to considerable differences in model predictions, it is important to inspect the behavior of modeled responses under different extrapolation strategies, which is rarely done in ENM studies. Such examination can help promote biologically realistic model transfers, for example by avoiding unconstrained extrapolation when the relevant tail of the modeled response has a sharply increasing trend. Here, we present a proposed workflow and new visualization tools to guide researchers in choosing appropriate extrapolation strategies, including plots for marginal response curves and non‐analog pixel densities. Making extrapolation choices individually for each tail per variable (‘custom clamping') helped avoid unrealistically high suitability predictions for non‐analog environments. This study emphasizes the importance of both inspecting response curves and assessing the total area with non‐analog conditions. Furthermore, we review the challenges that existing numerical models face in reflecting these changes and discuss possible solutions. We also propose an integrated mitigation strategy along the field–ditch–pond continuum to enhance pesticide removal efficiency at both stages. Finally, we identify key research priorities to guide future monitoring, modeling, and ecotoxicological assessments. title: Bamboo-based traditional bamboo market systems enhance rural livelihoods and ecosystem resilience in Karnataka
authors: G. M. Pavithra; G. V. Venkataramana; Sruthi Subbanna

A mixed-methods research approach was employed from 2017 to 2026 across eight districts of Karnataka (Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, Uttara Kannada, Shivamogga, Kodagu, Belagavi, Ballari, and Bidar). A stratified sampling approach was used with 16 respondents from each district, representing Traditional Bamboo Artisans (TBA), Adivasi and tribal communities, and small-scale entrepreneurs. Primary data collection involved semi-structured questionnaires capturing socio-economic and demographic characteristics, bamboo procurement sources, harvesting practices, and marketing strategies. Secondary data included population, literacy trends, and ecological stress indicators. Analysis combined comparative and descriptive methods with multivariable linear regression examining forest cover, annual rainfall, and forest area as predictors. Key findings revealed that bamboo dependence increases with proximity to forests, and better market access enables value addition, enterprise diversification, and strengthens indigenous knowledge systems. A four-zone Bamboo Value Chain Model (BVCM) was developed based on field observations, covering forest, rural, semi-urban, and craft-based systems, identifying market integration patterns at local scales through spatial zonation. The BVCM provides a quantitative and spatial framework for regional planning, market development, and sustainable management. The model highlights zone-specific strengths and gaps, enabling targeted interventions. Stronger policy support and institutional frameworks are essential for long-term sustainability across Karnataka.

title: Crucial tenants: the role of the microbiome in the North American bison (Bison bison) welfare, management and conservation
authors: Augusto Jacobo Montiel Castro; Karla Pelz Serrano; Genaro C. Miranda de la Lama; Rurik List
abstract: Following its near extinction over a century ago, the population of the North American bison has shown a remarkable recovery. However, a key biological aspect of its conservation has received little attention: its interdependence with its microbiome and its conjunction as a functional unit (i.e. a holobiont), which ultimately contributes to organismal welfare and health. When the organism’s microbiome and genome are functionally integrated, concurrently influencing its physiology, behavior, fitness and/or reproductive success, both should be considered as a single unit subject to natural selection. Therefore, as an influence on an individual´s capacity to cope with the challenges imposed by its environment, the multiple roles of the microbiome as an important link in the promotion of animal welfare, in this case, that of the North American bison ( Bison bison ), should be underscored. We aim to support this perspective by signaling bison’s physiological reliance on the gut microbiome, microbiome’s crucial role mediating stress from environmental and manage-related sources and the possibility to enhance its welfare by allowing natural social behaviors, and therefore, interindividual microbiome exchange to occur (including developmental microbiome priming early in life, through nursing). Our review thus highlights the relationship between bison and its microbiome as both a complement to current handling and management practices, and a valuable indicator for evaluating animal welfare. In this regard, it integrates physiological regulation, behavior and affective states, and suggests microbiome’s role as a key component for developing more effective and biologically informed conservation strategies.

title: Intraspecific genetic diversity as a driver of ecosystem functioning: trophic pathways, temporal dynamics, and conservation implications
authors: Arayaselassie Abebe Semu; Agegnehu Wasse Abegaz
abstract: Biodiversity research has historically emphasized species richness as a driver of ecosystem functioning, whereas intraspecific genetic diversity, the heritable variation within species has received comparatively less attention. Yet, genetic variation within species can influence productivity, nutrient cycling, community composition, trophic interactions, and ecosystem resilience. This review synthesizes empirical and theoretical evidence from terrestrial, freshwater, and marine systems to examine how intraspecific genetic diversity affects ecosystem processes across trophic levels and through time. Across the literature, the strongest evidence comes from systems dominated by foundation or keystone species, where genotype-dependent traits alter resource quality, habitat structure and species interactions, thereby generating cascading effects on herbivores, predators, decomposers, and associated microbial communities. These effects are particularly important under disturbance and environmental stress, and in several systems, they strengthen over time as trophic feedback accumulates. However, current knowledge remains taxonomically and geographically uneven, with temperate plant-based systems far better represented than tropical, microbial, freshwater, and deep-sea communities. Methodological heterogeneity in genetic metrics and experimental design also limits cross-study comparability. Further progress will depend on better integration of genomic tools with multi-trophic ecological experiments and long-term field studies. Recognizing and conserving intraspecific genetic diversity is therefore an evolutionary concern and a practical requirement for sustaining ecosystem resilience, restoration success, and climate adaptation.

title: Evaluating interspecific variation in biomass accumulation, carbon storage and soil quality within bamboo-based agroforestry in the western Himalayas
authors: Yourmila Kumari; D. R. Bhardwaj; Tarun Verma; Saurbh Shukla
abstract: Introduction Bamboo-based agroforestry systems have gained importance for their role in biomass production, carbon sequestration and soil enhancement under diverse ecological conditions. Methods The present study was conducted at the Regional Horticultural Research Station, Jachh (Himachal Pradesh), India in 8-year-old bamboo plantations to evaluate the growth performance, biomass accumulation, carbon dynamics and soil properties of five bamboo species Bambusa balcooa, Bambusa bambos, Dendrocalamus asper, Dendrocalamus hamiltonii and Dendrocalamus strictus under sub-montane low-hill conditions using a Randomized Block Design. Results B. bambos recorded the maximum culm diameter and culm height; whereas D. asper exhibited maximum culm density and live culms per clump. Maximum inter-nodal length (24.64 cm) was observed in B. balcooa . Biomass production was highest in B. bambos , resulting in the greatest total biomass (41.81 Mg ha −1 ), carbon concentration across plant components and improved soil properties. However, the highest aboveground (4.11 Mg ha -1 yr -1 ) and total carbon sequestration rates (4.50 Mg ha −1 yr −1 ) were recorded in D. hamiltonii , indicating greater annual carbon accumulation efficiency, while belowground carbon sequestration (0.49 Mg ha −1 yr −1 ) was highest in B. bambos . Leaf-litter deposition was maximum in B. bambos (1.14 and 0.65 kg m −2 before and after active growing season, respectively). Soil properties were significantly improved under B. bambos , with higher organic carbon, SOC stock, and available nutrients viz., N, P and K. Microbial biomass carbon (124.16 mg MB-C 100 g −1 soil) and microbial populations were also higher under B. bamboos . Overall, B. bambos emerged as the most productive species for biomass accumulation and soil improvement, while D. hamiltonii and D. strictus demonstrated higher carbon sequestration efficiency. Discussion These results highlight the species-specific potential of bamboo species in agroforestry systems for enhancing ecosystem productivity and climate change mitigation potential.

title: Carbon sink-source dynamics across ecuadorian coastal tropical dry forests: unraveling the seasonal balance of soil carbon inputs and CO2 efflux
authors: Emilio Jarre-Castro; Michael Macías-Pro; Roque Loor Dueñas; João Velez Velásquez; Carlos A. Salas-Macías; Ignacio J. Lorite; Ezequiel Zamora-Ledezma
abstract: Tropical dry forests play a crucial role in climate change mitigation by sequestering atmospheric carbon, yet the balance between soil carbon storage and soil CO 2 emissions remains poorly understood across contrasting forest subtypes. This study evaluated the seasonal carbon sink–source dynamics of three representative Ecuadorian coastal tropical dry forests by quantifying soil organic carbon (SOC), soil CO 2 efflux, and net carbon sink capacity (NCSC), while identifying the main edaphic drivers regulating these processes. Field measurements were conducted during the rainy and dry seasons in 12 permanent plots distributed across a Lowland Semideciduous Forest (LSF), a Deciduous Pacific Forest (DPF), and a Lowland Deciduous Forest and Shrubland (LDF). Soil organic carbon stocks, soil CO 2 efflux, soil physical and chemical properties, and vegetation diversity were quantified using standardized laboratory and field protocols. Annual SOC storage reached 11,439.96 Mg C yr −¹ in LSF, 327,111.22 Mg C yr −¹ in DPF, and 281,744.18 Mg C yr −¹ in LDF, whereas annual soil CO 2 emissions were substantially lower, totaling 1,876.46 Mg C yr⁻¹ in LSF, 80,353.00 Mg C yr −¹ in DPF, and 43,526.52 Mg C yr −¹ in LDF. Consequently, all three forest subtypes exhibited a positive Net Carbon Sink Capacity, confirming their role as net carbon sinks despite marked seasonal variability. Mean NCSC across the rainy and dry seasons was highest in LSF (56.6 Mg C ha −¹ ), followed by LDF (49.4 Mg C ha −¹ ) and DPF (47.0 Mg C ha −¹ ).These findings provide new evidence that Ecuadorian tropical dry forests maintain a positive carbon balance across contrasting climatic conditions and emphasize the importance of subtype-specific conservation and restoration strategies to maximize long-term carbon sequestration under climate change.

title: Reconnecting humans and nature through biocultural approaches: the role of indigenous cultural values for biodiversity conservation in Southwestern Nigeria
authors: Taiwo Kabiru Adebowale; Opemipo Alaba Ijose; Bosede Bolade Ibiyomi; Olukoya Oladapo Oduntan; Oluwasegun Kehinde Omoju; Oluwaferanmi Esther Ejibunu; Tolani Azeem Raji

A cross-sectional explanatory survey design was adopted, and data were collected from 395 respondents selected through a multistage sampling technique across eight Egba communities in Abeokuta North and Abeokuta South Local Government Areas, Ogun State. Significant age-related differences in perceptions of traditional conservation practices (p &lt; 0.05) highlighted generational variations in Indigenous ecological values. title: Comparative life cycle assessment of a year-round grazing system vs. a hay-feeding system
authors: K.R. Trumpp; J.C.B. Dubeux; A. Martin-Ryals; J. Portuguez Acuña; I.L. Bretas

title: Comparative life cycle assessment of plastic waste management technologies: Environmental performance of pyrolysis, mechanical recycling, chemical recycling and open burning
authors: Kripa Shrestha; Trang Luong; Pankaj Lal; Julia Fiore; Anuradha Singh; Cassidy Rucker; Rolih Ferdinand

title: The impacts of concurrent heatwaves and droughts on global wheat production and trade
authors: Elisabeth Vogel; Lily-belle Sweet; Andreia F S Ribeiro; Camille J Mora; Fiona Johnson; Jakob Zscheischler
abstract: Abstract Concurrent climate extremes in major crop-producing regions, such as synchronised droughts or heatwaves, threaten food security by causing simultaneous harvest failures. title: Is longer sonication worth the energy? Trade-offs between trimethoprim removal, toxicity, and biodegradability with initial assessment of impact on resistance genes

authors: Gonzalo Cortés-Capano; Anna Hausmann; Jacqueline Loos; Marcela Brugnach; Noelia Zafra-Calvo
abstract: Abstract Landscapes are relational and contested arenas where systemic crises, competing values and power asymmetries shape contested visions of sustainability. Conventional policy and technical responses often overlook how narratives and power relations legitimise particular futures while marginalising others. Using an illustrative fictional case, we show how the framework can surface hidden needs, expose assumptions about care and responsibilities, and highlight justice claims. The framework supports reflexive (re)narration attentive to plurality, positionality, conflict and democratic transformation pathways.

title: Balancing forage and fear: How people, environment and predators shape reindeer grazing in the Fennoscandian tundra
authors: Marianne Stoessel; Felicia Wikinger; Regina Lindborg
abstract: Abstract The long history of reindeer herding in Fennoscandia has shaped the mountain tundra by influencing its productivity, nutrient and carbon cycling and vegetation structure. By partly limiting shrub expansion, extensive reindeer grazing contributes to ecosystem resilience and helps mitigate climate change effects. Yet, outdoor tourism is discussed as a major pressure that can alter reindeer grazing patterns, with likely consequences cascading onto the tundra plant communities and vegetation structure. To study this, we tagged reindeer with GPS and accelerometers in three Swedish reindeer herding districts experiencing different levels of tourism pressure, and analysed their occurrence and grazing activity in relation to human infrastructures, habitat and predators. In the district with the highest tourism pressure, reindeer avoided large buildings but tolerated hiking trails. Responses were more mixed in the two other districts where large national hiking trails were avoided, but small cabins were not. Interestingly, the reindeer grazing patterns measured with accelerometers showed a different response to that inferred from reindeer occurrence alone, revealing that even where reindeer did not avoid human infrastructures, their grazing activity was still decreased. In all districts, we detected interactive effects between predators and human infrastructures, suggesting a ‘human‐shield’ effect at play, that is reindeer used the proximity to specific types of human infrastructure as a refuge from predation. This context‐dependent tolerance of reindeer towards humans according to predator presence reveals that even non‐lethal human presence in the mountains, in the form of tourism, can influence predator–prey interactions in the tundra. By decoupling spatially explicit grazing activities from presence‐only habitat selection, this study highlights that, even if reindeer might appear tolerant to human presence in the mountains, outdoor tourism can still disturb them by disrupting their grazing. As this study was conducted in a region experiencing substantial land use changes, our findings stress the need to better recognise the effects of human interactions with the tundra wildlife, particularly herbivores such as reindeer, as these can cascade onto other trophic levels and therefore affect broader ecosystem processes under climate change. title: Theories of care help explain a peri‐urban tree diversity paradox
authors: Jacqueline Hamilton; Murray M. Humphries; Heather Brown; Elena M. Bennett
abstract: Abstract Since diversity is often a management objective for peri‐urban tree communities on public land, one might expect to find greater diversity there than on private land, where such objectives are less common. Theories of care offer a novel lens for exploring how such relationships relate to tree diversity. We surveyed trees on private and public land in forest and non‐forest patches using 121 tree plots to compare diversity (species richness, evenness and size distribution). Through thematic analysis of 31 interviews associated with some of these plots, we explored expressions of tree care, including care about, taking care of, caregiving and care‐receiving. We asked how care varied and related to measurable differences in tree diversity. In forested patches, species diversity was high and there were no significant differences between private and public lands, suggesting landscape drivers are a primary force dictating tree diversity. In non‐forested patches, private plots had greater tree species richness than public lands and the only very large trees (>100 cm DBH). These diversity differences may reflect differences in non‐forest tree care, in addition to landscape drivers. Our findings reveal a paradox in which public land managers described tree diversity as an objective, yet non‐forested private lands, where no such objective existed, had greater diversity than public lands by most measures. Public land managers expressed care about native species and tree community resilience, while private landowners expressed care about particular trees, shaped by personal relationships, emotions and intergenerational efforts. Through explicitly considering care within a study of tree diversity, we found potential explanations for this paradox. Scale of responsibility and resources constrained some public tree care, while private tree care was emotionally satisfying and less constrained by institutional pressures. title: Shining light on the aurora's contributions to people: A qualitative study of the aurora borealis in Greenland
authors: James David Broome; David Cook; Brynhildur Davíðsdóttir; Benjamin David Hennig
abstract: Abstract The aurora borealis (northern lights) is an abiotic natural phenomenon that contributes to human well‐being. There is currently a significant research gap in primary qualitative valuation of the aurora's links to people. This exploratory qualitative study applies the Intergovernmental Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) framework in a novel context to study interactions between people and the aurora in Greenland. The main aims of the study are to: (1) identify nature's contribution to people (NCP) in Greenland from the aurora and (2) explore how local stakeholders can enhance management of NCP from the aurora. Drawing on 28 semi‐structured interviews conducted primarily in Ilulissat, Kulusuk and Tasiilaq, the aurora is found to provide benefits to people in a variety of ways. Benefits from the aurora span five NCP categories, including: energy, learning and inspiration, physical and psychological experiences, supporting identities and maintenance of options. The majority of benefits were non‐material in nature, although material benefits in the forms of tourism revenue and energy were also mentioned. Practical considerations are explored for the localities of Ilulissat in western Greenland and the Ammassalik region (Tasiilaq & Kulusuk) in eastern Greenland. These study sites vary in their social, economic and institutional profiles and demonstrate moderate heterogeneity in perceptions about co‐production and potential avenues for the management of NCP from the aurora. Ilulissat demonstrates a broad spectrum of potential for institutional co‐production, where there are considerable anthropogenic assets for underpinning NCP from the aurora. In contrast, Tasiilaq and Kulusuk demonstrate more purely relational values, where tourism‐related benefits are currently less developed. The information about aurora benefits and the role of co‐production elicited in this study can serve to support and inform decision‐making related to cultural heritage facilities, educational initiatives and tourism infrastructure pertaining to the aurora. Reflections about the usefulness of the IPBES framework in an abiotic context are discussed, and opportunities for future research are outlined. title: Curating landscapes to encourage care for biodiversity through arts and citizen science

abstract: Abstract This study investigates how combining Citizen Science and Art workshops within curated wildflower meadows can generate repeated, positive experiences with nature, and foster a sense of care for it. abstract: Abstract Green hydrogen has become a central pillar of net-zero strategies in Asia, but the gap between announced ambition and bankable demand is widening. Aggregate 2030 production targets across ten major Asian economies exceed 14 Mt yr-1, yet only 9% of the global low emissions hydrogen pipeline has reached a final investment decision. We apply a policy coherence analysis framework to 15 formally adopted national hydrogen strategies in Asia. Each strategy is scored on an ordinal scale across four dimensions: production credibility, demand integration, cross-sectoral coordination and public financing. The scoring framework is designed as a comparative governance heuristic rather than a predictive investment model. This can enable systematic comparison of institutional readiness across heterogeneous national contexts. Pairwise interactions among dimensions and across bilateral hydrogen agreements are then classified as reinforcing, neutral or constraining. Two main findings emerge from our analysis. First, demand integration lags every other dimension and participates in most of the constraining within-country interactions, which account for about one-fourth of pairwise combinations. Second, of twenty-five bilateral hydrogen and ammonia instruments coded for cross-country coherence, about 56% constrain the coherence of at least one signatory’s framework, and these instruments cluster on relationships with incumbent fossil fuel suppliers. Reinforcing agreements are concentrated on India-led and EU-facing renewable corridors. The pattern indicates a coherence trap rather than an ambition gap. The paper argues that the region’s principal governance challenge is not the absence of hydrogen ambition, but the uneven sequencing of policy development across supply and demand institutions. Addressing the resulting coherence gap requires governance interventions that strengthen domestic demand codification and align bilateral partnerships with emerging low-carbon demand architectures.

title: Invasive North American beaver alters greenhouse gas fluxes in sub-Antarctic riparian forests
authors: Julio A Salas-Rabaza; Carla Knappik; María Soledad Astorga-España; Brenda Riquelme-Del Río; José Luis Andrade; Frédéric Thalasso
abstract: Abstract The North American beaver ( Castor Canadensis ) has become a major invasive threat in the sub-Antarctic forests of the Fuegian Archipelago. By constructing dams, beavers flood and kill extensive forest areas, convert riparian forests (RFs) into wetlands, and substantially alter hydrological and biogeochemical processes. This study presents an integrated austral summer assessment of greenhouse gas(GHG) fluxes in a beaver-created wetland and an adjacent intact RF. Fluxes were measured from water, soil, and tree stem surfaces. CH 4 emissions were markedly higher in the beaver-degraded area than in the intact forest, with total ecosystem emissions of 20.36 and −1.59 mg CH 4 m −2 d −1 , respectively. In contrast, CO 2 emissions were greater in the intact RF (39.3 g CO 2 m −2 d −1 ) than in the beaver-degraded forest (4.32 g CO 2 m −2 d −1 ). Annualizing these summer fluxes yielded total GHG emissions that were 179 t CO 2-eq ha −1 yr −1 higher in the intact forest than in the beaver-created wetland. However, this difference does not account for forest gross primary production, which was not measured and for which no comparable estimates are available for sub-Antarctic forests. Consequently, although the intact RF likely functions as a net carbon sink, its magnitude could not be reliably estimated. In contrast, the beaver-created wetland, devoid of living trees, remained a net source of approximately 17 t CO 2-eq ha −1 yr −1 . These results indicate that beaver-induced deforestation may represent a substantial source of GHGs in southernmost forest ecosystems.

title: Economic impacts of California’s heat illness prevention policy
authors: Tina Duong Nguyen; Joe Simeone; Alina Schnake-Mahl; Leah H Schinasi
abstract: Abstract Mounting evidence indicates that heat stress in the workplace compromises economic activity. Workplace heat safety laws may be critical adaptive responses to mitigate these impacts. We evaluated the impact of California’s 2005 Heat Illness Prevention law, the first state-level workplace heat safety policy enacted in the United States, on economic activity. We used county- and year-stratified, inflation-adjusted per-capita payroll in heat-exposed industries from the US Census Bureau’s Business Patterns Data to assess economic activity. We linked these to county- and yearly heat shocks (number of days that exceeded 27 °C or 32 °C), calculated using 4 km-resolution daily meteorological data from Oregon State University’s PRISM group. We used county-industry fixed effects linear regression models, adjusted for annual precipitation and cold shocks, to estimate associations between heat shocks and payroll per capita, before (2000–2004) and after (2005–2010) enactment of California’s heat illness prevention standard, in CA counties ( N = 58) compared with Oregon (OR) ( N = 36), where a policy did not exist. We stratified analyses by climate zone. In CA, each additional day that exceeded 27 °C was associated with a 0.05% reduction in payroll per capita (95% CI: −0.17%, 0.08%), pre-policy enactment, and with a 0.07% increase in payroll per capita (95% CI: −0.07%, 0.20%), post-enactment. Associations were stronger in temperate counties. CA vs OR associations, however, were not markedly different, and most estimates of association were imprecise. Although imprecise, this first-of-its-kind analysis provided suggestive evidence that workplace heat safety policies do not impair, and in some cases, may improve county-level economic activity. These results contribute to the ongoing debate over the adoption of workplace heat safety standards. Future studies in different settings and using more temporally granular data are needed to confirm these results.

title: Windows of opportunity in the prediction of dry and wet seasonal climate anomalies: a case study for the Middle East in autumn
authors: Thomas Dal Monte; Andrea Alessandri; Annalisa Cherchi; Markus Donat; Marco Gaetani
abstract: Abstract Seasonal prediction of dry and wet events remains a major challenge in climate science, particularly in semi-arid regions such as the Middle East, where water security is tightly related to precipitation variability. Identifying ‘ windows of opportunity ’-i.e. space and time domains where large-scale teleconnections may enhance predictability-is crucial to enable the timely issuance of early warnings for vulnerable regions during critical rainy seasons. In this study, windows of opportunity are explored over the Middle East by assessing the contribution of each autumn to the prediction skill for precipitation across eight seasonal prediction systems (SPSs) and their multi-model ensembles. Our results reveal that a small number of years, characterized by strong anomalies in the tropical Pacific or the Indian Ocean, are the main contributors to the prediction skill of dry and wet events in the Middle East. By comparing the performances of the SPSs, we show that the relative skill in predicting dry and wet events increases together with the respective ability of individual SPSs to represent the relevant large-scale teleconnections. This can significantly increase the practical value of seasonal predictions in climate-vulnerable regions.

title: Enhanced seasonal soil moisture forecasts by integrating APCC multi-model ensemble predictions into a land surface model framework
authors: Chanhyuk Choi; Min-Seok Kim; Jin-Ho Yoon; Hyungjun Kim; Jee-Hoon Jeong
abstract: Abstract Soil moisture is a key driver of climate variability and extremes such as heatwaves and wildfires, and accurate prediction at seasonal timescales is therefore essential. Skillful forecasts at these scales, however, remain a significant challenge. While multi-model ensemble (MME) climate forecasts consistently outperform individual models for atmospheric variables, their soil moisture outputs require careful interpretation when combined across models because of differences in land surface model (LSM) structures and soil configurations. To bridge this gap, we developed a seasonal soil moisture prediction system using the Joint UK Land Environment Simulator driven by NCEP CFSv2 meteorological forecasts, and integrated monthly temperature and precipitation forecasts from the APCC MME—which exhibits superior seasonal prediction skill to single dynamical models—into the system’s meteorological forcing. Despite correcting only temperature and precipitation—the two variables consistently available across all participating MME models—the approach yielded substantial improvements in soil moisture forecast skill. Retrospective hindcast experiments for 1991–2016, initialized in February, show that the MME-corrected forecast (J-MME) substantially outperforms the CFSv2-driven baseline (J-CFSv2) in predicting boreal spring–summer soil moisture. The global average coefficient of determination ( R 2 ) between forecast and reanalysis increased by 0.10–0.12 at three- to four-month lead times. The improvements were driven by precipitation correction in water-limited regions and temperature correction in energy-limited high-latitude regions. This approach also extended the effective lead time for statistically significant predictions and improved the detection of historical drought events, demonstrating that even limited integration of MME information into an LSM framework can yield meaningful gains in seasonal soil moisture and drought forecasting.

title: An empirical socio-economic indicator of country-level food security
authors: Davide Castellani; Alessandro Tavoni; Paolo D’Odorico
abstract: Abstract Economic access is a central dimension of food security, yet cross-country empirical work has limited measures that link the purchasing power of low-income populations to food expenditure across countries. We introduce the socio-economic index of food security (SEF), defined as the ratio between the per capita income of the bottom 20 percent of the income distribution and average per capita food expenditure. Using data from 110 countries, we examine the ability of SEF to explain cross-country differences in the prevalence of undernourishment (PoU), the Food and Agriculture Organization indicator of insufficient dietary energy intake. SEF explains a substantial share of cross-country variation in undernourishment. On average, a 1 percent increase in SEF is associated with a 0.25 percent lower PoU. The relationship is non-linear, with quantile regressions showing stronger effects at higher levels of food insecurity, where estimated elasticities range from − 0.19 at the 25th percentile to − 0.34 at the 95th percentile. Interestingly, an affordability measure based on the purchasing power of the poorest quintile captures cross-country differences in dietary-energy undernourishment more accurately than measures based on national-average income. SEF is therefore best understood as a globally comparable indicator of economic access to food, complementing household-level and multidimensional food security measures.

title: Towards a sub-seasonal climate forecast service for extreme precipitation associated with cut-off lows: insights from the Valencia 2024 event
authors: Núria Pérez-Zanón; Diego A Campos; Ramiro I Saurral; Francisco J Doblas-Reyes; Albert Soret
abstract: Abstract Cut-off lows (COLs) are a major driver of high-impact precipitation events at mid-latitudes, yet their predictability at sub-seasonal timescales remains limited. This study evaluates sub-seasonal forecasts of accumulated precipitation and large-scale atmospheric conditions for the COL that affected Valencia on 29 October 2024, with the aim of assessing forecast products that could support earlier anticipation of such events. After applying a COL detection algorithm, two forecast product definitions are explored for this event. First, the odds ratio, which compares forecast probability with climatological frequency, provided spatially consistent indications of increased likelihood of COL prediction up to two weeks in advance, although the Brier Skill Score showed limited and often non-significant skill at longer lead times. Second, the odds is accompanied by the Odds Ratio Skill Score, which remains stable for rare events. However, no clear signal was evident earlier than one week in advance. The results highlight the potential of the forecast product based on the odds ratio definition of COL detection to complement precipitation forecasts. These products could support earlier preparedness when co-designed with end-users, especially in regions where COLs can lead to damaging precipitation.

title: Large-scale circulation-conditioned attribution of the historic 2024 Spanish extreme precipitation
authors: Mengyuan Yao; Haosu Tang; Gang Huang; Jun Wang
abstract: Abstract On 29 October 2024, Turís, Spain, recorded an unprecedented 24 h precipitation total of 771 mm, triggering one of the deadliest floods in Europe since 1900. Although recent attribution studies demonstrated that anthropogenic warming may have contributed to the event, the extent to which atmospheric circulation variability shaped its exceptional magnitude remains unclear. Using multi-source high-resolution precipitation observations, this study uncovers the dynamical and thermodynamical mechanisms driving the event. The exceptional precipitation was initiated by an anomalously deep upper-level cut-off low over southern Spain, accompanied by a southeasterly jet that enhanced the transport of warm, moisture-laden air from the Mediterranean. Circulation analog analysis reveals that pre-trough dynamics explain ∼31% (interquartile range: 7%–44%) of the maximum daily precipitation across eastern Spain during October–November 2024. Large-ensemble attribution using the HadGEM3-A-N216 model further confirms the crucial role of internal dynamics, which account for approximately one-third of the total anomaly, while the remaining signal is dominated by the combined contribution of anthropogenic forcing and internal thermodynamic processes. These results highlight the important role of atmospheric circulation in shaping Mediterranean precipitation extremes, emphasizing the need for explicitly accounting for circulation variability in event attribution and future regional flood risk assessment.

title: A quantitative evaluation of forest aboveground biomass density map products in Oregon, USA
authors: Andrew T Hudak; Jennifer L Bakken; Andrew Lister; Francisco Mauro; Matthew J Gregory; Karin Riley; Barry Wilson; Maurizio Santoro; Sean Healey; Lei Ma; Yifan Yu; Benjamin C Bright; John Byrne; Roy Mita; Rachel M Houtman; John D Shaw; Patrick A Fekety; Grant Domke; Brian Walters; David M Bell; Aaron Weiskittel; Jeff W Atkins; Laura Duncanson; Neha Hunka; Robert Kennedy; Chad Babcock; Sassan Saatchi; Brett Raczka; Carlos Silva; Hao Tang; George Hurtt
abstract: Abstract Maps of aboveground biomass density (AGBD) estimated from remote sensing data with models trained from inventory data are essential for carbon monitoring. Forest inventory plots in the United States (US) are measured by the forest inventory and analysis (FIA) program of the US Forest Service (USFS). These plots are spatially representative, design unbiased, and provide estimates of AGBD and other forest attributes over large spatial domains, but do not provide spatially continuous or sufficiently precise estimates over small spatial domains (e.g. forest stands). Integration with remote sensing can fill this gap, but remote sensing cannot measure AGBD directly, so models predicting ground-measured AGBD as a function of remote sensing data are often used to generate maps. We evaluated 10 alternative types of AGBD maps that used LiDAR, multispectral satellite (Landsat) image time series, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), or alternative modeling approaches. We evaluated the agreement between mapped AGBD predictions and AGBD observations collected at the FIA plots or in stands surveyed on USFS lands. Ground observations were regressed on mapped AGBD predictions at different spatial aggregation levels: county, 64 000-ha FIA sample hexagon, stand polygon, FIA plot, and FIA subplot (unaggregated). Standardized major axis regression model fit statistics were calculated and compared to evaluate the map products across the study area, a large portion of western and central Oregon. Based on these fit statistics, we found that the Landsat-derived maps performed best at the coarser evaluation levels (county, hexagon), airborne LiDAR-based products performed best at finer evaluation levels (stand, plot, subplot), and the SAR-dominated products showed lower agreement with ground-based AGBD estimates in this high-biomass Oregon study area. When choosing between AGBD map types, we recommend map users consider the scale of their decision space as much as type of remote sensing data or modeling approach used in map production.

title: Analyzing land characteristics associated with historical large-scale solar photovoltaic deployment in the united states
authors: Jianyu Gu; Jordan Macknick; Ben Hoen; Jay E Diffendorfer; K Sydny Fujita; Zachary H Ancona; James McCall; Dylan Harrison-Atlas
abstract: Abstract Large-scale solar (LSS) deployment has accelerated rapidly across the United States, yet comprehensive understanding of its siting patterns remains limited. Here, we present a national-scale geospatial assessment of land characteristics converted for LSS development and apply statistical analyses to evaluate whether installations are disproportionately concentrated within specific land types. We find that siting patterns are strongly correlated with high solar irradiance, underscoring the role of resource quality in shaping deployment decisions. LSS projects are disproportionately concentrated on agricultural lands and shrubland. Within agricultural areas, installations predominantly occur on croplands and are strongly associated with irrigated systems. Notably, more than 90% of projects are deployed on agricultural land with Productive, Versatile, and Resilient (PVR) index values of land quality exceeding the national median. These findings highlight the need for strategic siting frameworks that reconcile solar development with the conservation of agriculturally valuable land.

authors: Valerie J. Cornet; Scott F. Heron; Karen E. Joyce
abstract: Abstract Coral bleaching is primarily driven by heat stress, yet additional environmental factors, such as nutrient availability and light attenuation, can affect bleaching severity. Using Generalised Additive Models, we tested multiple chlorophyll a metrics (mean, maximum, minimum, and cumulative sum) across different time frames (3–12 weeks) to determine their predictive value. In contrast, at offshore reefs, where oligotrophic conditions dominate, chlorophyll a fluctuations likely reflected upwelling-induced cooling and moderate nutrient enrichment, initially buffering corals from bleaching but increasing severity when excessive accumulation occurred. Long-term chlorophyll a metrics (9–12-week mean and cumulative sum) improved predicted bleaching (adj. R 2 = 0.55–0.57) compared to heat stress alone (adj. title: Abrupt changes in grassland productivity induced by shrub encroachment
authors: Yiyin Liu; Jingyi Ding; Wenwu Zhao; Jingjing Meng; Jinyu Wang; Weiling Niu; David J. Eldridge

title: Demographic responses to population recovery illustrated by 30 years of monitoring a once critically endangered parrot

title: Enabling Nature‐Based Solutions by Embracing Their Limits: Insights From Governing in Complexity
authors: Kerry A. Waylen; Rakhyun E. Kim
abstract: ABSTRACT Nature‐based solutions (NbS) have become a central concept in contemporary conservation. While much scholarship and practice aim to refine and upscale NbS, we argue that it is important to recognize their inherent limits, which stem from the complexity of socio‐ecological systems. These manifest as recurrent limits for NbS, including shifting priorities, unavoidable trade‐offs, recurring conflicts, unexpected outcomes, external shocks, and contested knowledge. title: Fostering a network for creating and implementing open education resources in ecology

(c) Peer review is conducted through a living collaborative model rather than a static editorial review. (d) Embedded real‐time data tools use applications that incorporate actual field datasets collected by the module authors. title: Spatially realistic dynamic N‐mixture models
authors: Qing Zhao; Paige E. Howell; Erin Muths; Brent H. Sigafus; Blake R. Hossack; Christopher E. Latimer
abstract: Abstract Dispersal is a complex ecological process that can be driven by the abiotic environment, density‐dependent processes and species mobility. Using simulations, we evaluated the inferential performance of this model when large proportions of sites are unsurveyed and the survey period is short, situations that are typical of real‐world studies. The case study of Common Nighthawks showed the ability of the model to reveal the effect of primary productivity on dispersal and to map dispersal across the study area. authors: Juan C. Diaz‐Ricaurte; Marcio Martins
abstract: Abstract Thermal traits are central to understanding how ectotherms respond to environmental warming. However, not all thermal traits describe the same biological process. The system consists of a controlled heating chamber, an escape zone, thermocouples and continuous temperature recording. This design allows researchers to record body temperature at the moment of voluntary withdrawal while controlling heating rate and monitoring internal chamber conditions. We describe the construction, assembly, calibration and scaling of the VTMaxBox and provide open‐source design files to facilitate replication and adaptation. We also outline a recommended experimental workflow, including animal acclimation, chamber stabilization, heating‐rate control, endpoint definition and data extraction. We further discuss the performance, limitations and appropriate applications of the VTMaxBox. Its use requires careful standardization of chamber size, ramping rate, animal handling and ethical safeguards. title: The superposition method for the reconstruction of food webs
authors: Ettore Barbieri; Naoto F. Ishikawa
abstract: Abstract Understanding trophic positions is essential for analysing complex food webs. While calculating these positions can be straightforward when feeding relationships and their proportions are known, determining diet coefficients traditionally requires substantial time and effort. Stable isotope analysis provides trophic position estimates, but this information alone does not reveal prey–predator relationships. Our method employs a superposition of potential prey pairs, with weighting coefficients given by probabilities computed using Bayesian statistics. We present a mathematical inverse analysis approach to estimate diet coefficients using a minimal dataset consisting only of trophic positions. This approach provides a robust and parsimonious framework for reconstructing potential feeding networks from minimal data, offering a quantitative bridge between, but not limited to, stable isotope measurements and ecological network structure.

title: Forecasting ecological trajectories from ecological dynamic regimes to improve resilience analysis
authors: Martina Sánchez‐Pinillos; Marie‐Josée Fortin; Christian Messier; Daniel Kneeshaw
abstract: Abstract The ecological dynamic regime (EDR) framework was recently proposed as an alternative to equilibrium‐based approaches for assessing ecological resilience in empirical systems, explicitly incorporating dynamic regimes as a reference for assessing the system's deviation during disturbances. title: Spatial signatures of group cohesion
authors: Nicola E. Love; Sarah P. Otto
abstract: Abstract Wildlife populations are undergoing unprecedented changes to their spatial distributions as a result of human activities. title: Measuring stabilized heart rates in the prairie lizard, a small vertebrate ectotherm
authors: Owen Conroy; Brandon Wolfsohn; Garret Peterson; Tiffany Hegdahl; Travis R. Robbins
abstract: Abstract The ability to accurately measure heart rates is vital for studying the ecological and evolutionary pressures on animals because cardiovascular regulation is associated with key physiological responses to environmental change. Heart rates, especially in ectotherms, are influenced by multiple factors over both the short and long term, including environmental temperatures, handling frequency, metabolic rates and hemodynamic demands. title: Novel class identification: A human‐in‐the‐loop approach for efficient species recognition in bioacoustic data
authors: Hannes Kath; Thiago S. Gouvêa; Daniel Sonntag

title: Contrastive ecoacoustic indices: Large‐scale global soundscape characterization with contrastive inference

title: An efficient Bayesian phylogenetic approach for joint inference of continuous and discrete trait evolution under a state‐dependent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model
authors: Priscilla Lau; Bjørn T. Kopperud; John T. Clarke; Dirk Metzler; Sebastian Höhna

title: Better defining habitat patches to improve spatially explicit modelling outputs

title: <scp>ESO</scp> : An evolutionary algorithm for efficient model reduction via automated frequency band selection in passive acoustic monitoring

title: Phylogenetic structure of conifers in regional floras in relation to climate and environmental heterogeneity worldwide
authors: Hong Qian; Michael Kessler; Shenhua Qian
abstract: Despite having only about 670 species worldwide, conifers are one of the ecologically and economically most important plant groups. They have a rich fossil record and previous studies have shown that their current diversity is the result of past radiations, extinction, and dispersal events, restricting many genera to either the Northern or Southern Hemisphere, and concentrating species richness in specific regions. However, it remains poorly explored how this translates into patterns of phylogenetic diversity. In this study, we used a species‐level megaphylogeny and species lists for 391 geographic units worldwide to calculate six metrics of phylogenetic diversity and disparity, and to relate these to climatic factors. We found that the different metrics provided different patterns, reflecting deep and shallow evolutionary history, but that overall southeastern China had the highest values. We also found that patterns of phylogenetic diversity and disparity were better explained by current than historical climate, by temperature‐ than precipitation‐related variables, and by climatic seasonality than by climatic extremes. These patterns differ in many important regards from those known from ferns and angiosperms. Most notably, species‐poor conifer assemblages tend to have high phylogenetic dispersion, being composed of few species belonging to distinct lineages, rather than few lineages with many species each, as is typical for ferns and angiosperms. We conclude that the ecological and evolutionary processes determining community assembly in conifers differ fundamentally from those seen in ferns and angiosperms, reflecting their low global species richness.

title: Global distribution of avian plumage coloration and patterning: the relative influence of climate, ecology, and sexual selection
authors: Yuqing Han; Ying Zeng; Tien Ming Lee; Long Wang; Chen Zeng; Pengfei Fan; Çağan H. Şekercioğlu; Weini Huang; Yang Liu
abstract: Animal coloration exhibits substantial biogeographic variation, reflecting complex adaptations to both abiotic and biotic environments. To test ecogeographical predictions, we modeled variation in plumage lightness, blue–yellow chromaticity, and pattern granularity using phylogenetic mixed models and path analyses. Our analyses revealed pronounced geographic heterogeneity in both plumage coloration and patterning. Variation in plumage lightness followed broad climatic gradients, and darker coloration was associated with humid and colder environments, consistent with the combined predictions of Gloger's rule (darker in warm, humid areas) and Bogert's rule (darker in cold areas). These rules are not contradictory but coexist; their relative influence is determined by whether humidity or temperature is the dominant selective force in a given region. Furthermore, we identified a strong latitudinal gradient along the blue–yellow axis: tropical humidity promotes carotenoid‐rich yellow plumage through dietary shifts, whereas higher latitudes favor structural blue hues. Patterning also showed large‐scale structure, with larger pattern elements linked to humid environments and larger body sizes rather than to specific foraging habitats. By integrating classical ecological rules with the thermoregulation hypothesis, our study provides a unified framework explaining how climatic constraints and ecological processes interact to shape the global distribution of avian coloration patterns.

title: Continental scale metagenomics reveals Microcystis ‐induced synchrony among aquatic taxa is exacerbated by trophic cascades
authors: Lemian Liu; Siqi Zhu; Xiaoqin Huang; Wenjia Hu; Lixiang Luo; Xiusong Pan; Jianfeng Chen

title: The dual influence of top‐down and bottom‐up processes on a mesopredator and the consequences for prey
authors: Camilla Wikenros; Emelie Sabrie; , Gunnar Jansson; Henrik Andrén
abstract: Ecosystem dynamics are shaped by interacting top‐down and bottom‐up processes, yet their relative importance may vary through time following disturbances such as disease outbreaks and changes in apex predator communities. Potential drivers of fox dynamics (number of litters) were vole Clethrionomys glareolus and Microtus agrestis abundance, sarcoptic mange outbreaks, and the re‐establishment of Eurasian lynx Lynx lynx and wolves Canis lupus , and we assessed potential subsequent effects on hare Lepus europaeus and L. timidus and woodland grouse Lyrurus tetrix and Tetrao urogallus densities. Fox litter numbers were positively associated with vole abundance throughout the study period, indicating persistent bottom‐up regulation. In contrast, top‐down effects were evident through reductions in the number of fox litters during sarcoptic mange outbreaks and following the simultaneous presence of lynx and wolves. Moreover, the characteristic synchrony between voles and secondary prey weakened following the return of apex predators, suggesting direct and indirect effects beyond mesopredator suppression. Our results demonstrate that fox reproduction is regulated by concurrent top‐down and bottom‐up processes and that apex predator recovery can alter trophic relationships and not only reverse mesopredator release.

title: Climatic niche divergence and high‐elevation adaptation promoted rapid diversification of Pimoa spiders in Pan‐Himalaya
authors: Xiaoqing Zhang; Zhe Zhao; Bingyue Zhu; Tongyao Jiang; Lili Shao; Stefano Mammola; Jiangni Li; Hao Xu; Bing Li; Shuqiang Li

Notably, in the Pan‐Himalaya, Pimoa occurs at significantly higher elevations and exhibits far greater species diversity than in the other two regions, making it an ideal model for studying invertebrate diversification in this area. title: Community‐level egg and larval trait interactions with the Amazon River plume determine its role as a dispersal barrier
authors: Ramon B. Santos; Nelson A. Gouveia; Douglas F. M. Gherardi
abstract: The Amazon River plume (ARP) functions as a dynamic and porous biogeographic barrier whose permeability to larval dispersal depends on the interplay between species' biological traits and oceanographic processes. Diel vertical migration (DVM) was the second biological key factor (11%), modulating whether larvae were locally retained (with DVM) or exported to distant regions (without DVM). Seasonality and the geographic context of spawning habitats further shaped larval interactions with the plume, reinforcing the spatial and temporal complexity of this system. Overall, the ARP acts not as an absolute barrier but as a continuum of permeability, a selective filter that restricts dispersal of eggs and larvae of coastal species with short PLDs and low physiological tolerance, yet facilitates exchange for communities with greater dispersal capacity and behavioral plasticity.

title: Dietary partitioning mediates species coexistence in the high seas area of northwest Pacific
authors: Na Zang; Bilin Liu; Wenjun Zheng; Yushuang Luo; André E. Punt; Xinjun Chen; Dongming Lin
abstract: Niche partitioning, manifesting along various axes of the ecological niche, is a fundamental mechanism mediating species coexistence in a system. However, the emergence of many species in marine ecosystems would face considerable constraints in achieving coexistence through spatiotemporal differentiation mechanisms under the framework of niche partitioning. We measured the bulk carbon and nitrogen stable isotopes and essential fatty acids of the nine species to estimate the isotopic and nutritional niche spaces, and employed Hutchinson's n‐dimensional hypervolume framework to examine the degree of dietary specialization. Results revealed that pairwise overlap of isotopic niches was observed for all species, though some species occupied distinct isotopic niche spaces. In contrast, the nutritional niche space, estimated using essential fatty acids, was mostly separate for each species, coupled with small or zero overlap between paired species. Furthermore, the specialization index, estimated using either stable isotopes or essential fatty acids, was consistently large for the nine species, while nestedness was relatively low. These findings reveal that the nine species partition their nutritional niche spaces to mitigate the competition caused by dietary niche overlaps, coinciding with the mechanism of dietary specialization.

title: Combining paleoecology and modeling to explore cascading disturbances in forest ecosystems
authors: Cécile C. Remy; Matthew D. Hurteau; Sarah Le Berre; Dominik Thom; Rupert Seidl; Laurent Millet; Damien Rius
abstract: Climate‐induced cascading disturbance interactions pose a major challenge to the sustainable provision of forest ecosystem services to society. title: Increase in plant productivity in the tundra in Sweden is not related to increasing presence of warm‐adapted vascular plant species
authors: Tim Horstkotte; Jakob Assmann; Henrik Hedenås; Signe Normand; Johan Olofsson
abstract: Over the past decades, Arctic and alpine biomes have warmed faster than the global average. At a local and regional level, however, reported vegetation changes are much more variable. We first investigated changes in vegetation productivity by analysing the trend in the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI). However, warm‐adapted forbs increased more than cold‐adapted species. We conclude that, although part of the vascular vegetation is getting more thermophilic, the observed increase in vegetation productivity during the last two decades is not driven by an increase in warm‐adapted species. We also suggest that reindeer grazing, which occurs in almost the entire study region, contributes to the preservation of cold‐adapted Arctic–alpine biodiversity by selectively feeding on warm‐adapted vascular species.

title: Global analysis suggests nitrogen deposition as an underestimated driver of vegetation greening
authors: Jonas Trepel; Joe Atkinson; Oliver Baines; Matthew Kerr; Elizabeth le Roux; Hannah Rubin; Jens‐Christian Svenning; Robert Buitenwerf
abstract: The local effects of atmospheric nitrogen deposition on plants are well established, yet a global empirical analysis of nitrogen deposition effects on vegetation dynamics is missing. Although EVI increased slightly slower inside PAs, protection status did not alter the relationship between nitrogen deposition and greening. title: The Biodiversity of Retreating Glaciers Leaves an Ecological Legacy in Emerging Soil Communities

title: Fire–Moisture Interactions Shape Recovery Trajectories Across Temperate Vegetation Communities
authors: Emily K. Simpson; Glenda M. Wardle; Christopher R. Dickman; Aaron C. Greenville

Closing these gaps offers a unique opportunity to translate decades of scientific progress into next‐generation mitigation strategies that align agricultural productivity with climate stabilization goals.

title: Global Change Impacts on Mineral‐Associated Organic Matter: Consequences for Soil Carbon Persistence
authors: Juan Jia; Xiaojuan Feng
abstract: ABSTRACT Mineral‐associated organic matter (MAOM) in soils constitutes the largest terrestrial carbon pool and the primary reservoir of soil nitrogen. title: Arboreal Mammals Are at Risk Under Climate Change: Insights From a Global Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
authors: Dinayadura Kalathma Navanjalie Samanthi De Silva; Carly Campbell; Grant Hamilton
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate change poses significant threats to biodiversity, altering species survival and interactions within diverse ecological networks. title: Pollination Under Pressure: Grazing and Nutrient Enrichment Reshape Arctic Pollinator Communities and Interaction Networks

title: Continental‐Scale Biodiversity Predictions Are Influenced by Climatic Variability and Extreme Weather
authors: Jeremy M. Cohen; Diego Ellis‐Soto; Shubhi Sharma; Frank A. La Sorte; Walter Jetz
abstract: ABSTRACT Increasingly variable and extreme weather can push organisms beyond their physiological thermal or hydric tolerances and limit where they can persist, affecting their geographic distributions and biodiversity patterns. authors: Oliver Link; Stefan M. Jahnel; Kristin Janicek; Daniel Guerguerian; Johanna Kraus; Juan D. Montenegro; Bob Zimmermann; Brittney Wick; Konstantin Khalturin; Alison G. Cole; Ulrich Technau
abstract:
by Oliver Link, Stefan M. Jahnel, Kristin Janicek, Daniel Guerguerian, Johanna Kraus, Juan D. Montenegro, Bob Zimmermann, Brittney Wick, Konstantin Khalturin, Alison G. Cole, Ulrich Technau

The life cycle of most medusozoan cnidarians is marked by the metagenesis from the asexually reproducing sessile polyp and the sexually reproducing motile medusa. At present, it is unknown to what extent this drastic morphological transformation is accompanied by molecular changes in the cell type composition. Here, we provide a single-cell transcriptome atlas of the cosmopolitan scyphozoan Aurelia coerulea focusing on changes in individual cell states during the transition from polyp to medusa. Notably, this transition is marked by an increase in cell type diversity, including an expansion of neural subtypes and the appearance of striated muscles. We find that two families of neuronal lineages are specified by homologous transcription factors in the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis and A. coerulea, suggesting an origin in the common ancestor of medusozoans and anthozoans about 500 Myr ago. Our analysis suggests that gene duplications might be drivers for the increase of cellular complexity during the evolution of cnidarian neuroglandular lineages and highlights the close relationship of neurons and muscles. One key medusozoan-specific cell type is the striated muscle in the subumbrella. Evaluating muscle types by fiber anatomy and gene expression validation of their individual molecular profiles made it possible for the first time to investigate transcriptome differences between smooth and striated muscles. Although smooth and striated muscles are phenotypically different, both have a similar regulation of the contractile complex, reminiscent to the regulation of smooth muscles in bilaterians. This contrasts with bilaterian striated muscles, where the regulation of muscle contraction involves Ca2+ binding troponins and their interaction with Tropomyosin. These data suggest that smooth muscle contraction regulation is ancestral and the use of troponins in striated muscles only evolved in bilaterians.

title: Lateralised neural mechanisms facilitate auditory self-other distinction and coordination in human dyads
authors: Manuel Varlet; Tomas Lenc; Sylvie Nozaradan; David Poeppel; Peter E. Keller
abstract:
by Manuel Varlet, Tomas Lenc, Sylvie Nozaradan, David Poeppel, Peter E. Keller

Coordinating actions with others is essential for successful social interaction. Such coordination, as in sports and musical performances, often relies on sound, requiring the brain to process and integrate acoustic information related to the actions of ‘self’ and ‘other’ while maintaining sufficient distinction between them. However, such self-other differentiation can be challenged during real-world auditory interactions due to self and other signals being mixed when arriving at the eardrum, creating the potential for agency confusion and impaired coordination. Here we combined dual-EEG and frequency tagging techniques to investigate the behavioural and brain mechanisms supporting the self-other distinction during a joint auditory-motor synchronisation task. The results revealed better synchronisation when participants were associated with distinct sounds (different frequency and brightness) and designated leadership roles, facilitating the processing of self and other information and their separation at both peripheral and central levels. The results also indicated that this neural facilitation was stronger in the right hemisphere than the left, as well as for self than other, suggesting critical roles of spectral information and control over one’s own actions for auditory self-other distinction and coordination. These findings highlight complementary behavioural and brain mechanisms compensating for self-other masking inherent to auditory interactions, opening new avenues to understanding interpersonal coordination and its disorders.

title: Mental health help-seeking in New York City: How intersecting identities shape informal and formal support use
authors: Thinh Toan Vu; Jo-Anne Caton; Christina Norman
abstract:
by Thinh Toan Vu, Jo-Anne Caton, Christina Norman

This study investigated how intersecting identities, including race and ethnicity, gender, socioeconomic status, and immigration-related characteristics, impact help-seeking for emotions, nerves, or mental health among New York City (NYC) adults. title: A dual-polarized RIS-assisted spatial modulation architecture for robust vehicular communications in urban environments

abstract:

title: Family accommodation in childhood, adolescent, and young adult cancer survivors: A scoping review protocol
authors: Rinat Nissim; Rouhi Fazelzad; Sarah Daniels; Jake Heinbuch; Aditya Lumb; Luke Heinbuch; Andreea A. Manea; Uri Berger
abstract:
by Rinat Nissim, Rouhi Fazelzad, Sarah Daniels, Jake Heinbuch, Aditya Lumb, Luke Heinbuch, Andreea A. Manea, Uri Berger

title: Maternal early warning system (MEWS) model for predicting and reducing severe maternal outcomes in Ethiopia
authors: Saba Desta Tessema; Mesfin Tadese; Solomon Hailemeskel; Chaltu Takele Mule; Getaneh Dejen Tiche; Lidya Asalefew Mekonnen; Getnet Mitike Kassie
abstract:
by Saba Desta Tessema, Mesfin Tadese, Solomon Hailemeskel, Chaltu Takele Mule, Getaneh Dejen Tiche, Lidya Asalefew Mekonnen, Getnet Mitike Kassie

Maternal mortality in Ethiopia remains high, while most of these deaths are preventable. Early detection of deterioration and prompt response are essential to reduce these preventable deaths. A parallel, quasi-experimental study design was conducted among 1138 obstetric inpatients at four public hospitals of North Shewa Zone, Ethiopia. The recruitment period was from 05/05/2025–31/8/2025. The control group (n = 569) received the standard clinical monitoring. title: Evaluating genetic diversity differences within a likelihood framework
authors: David C. Nickle
abstract:
by David C. Nickle

title: CT-PestNet: A novel crop pest classification model based on cross-scale feature distillation enhancement and vision transformer with local token interaction

abstract:

title: Reafferent origins of image-forming vision
authors: Abraham Englander; Eva Jablonka
abstract: We propose that reafference was central to the evolution of image-forming vision. On this view, reafferent control over optic flow was the key innovation that made light a usable sense for directed navigation; progressive improvements in circuits, wiring, and optics then transformed residual contrast maps (“proto-images”) into spatial vision. title: Origins of termite eusociality: developmental foundations
authors: Christine A. Nalepa
abstract: Hemimetaboly and an extraordinarily flexible caste system are two features that that make termites, the eusocial cockroaches, distinct from the Hymenoptera. title: Future NDVI projections and ensemble strategy comparison in Inner Mongolia under CMIP6 scenarios
authors: Haoran Li; Yimei He; Qingqing Li; Yu Liu; Xiaoyi Ma
abstract: Introduction Accurate projections of future vegetation dynamics are essential for understanding ecosystem responses to climate change and developing adaptation strategies in arid and semi-arid regions. Two ensemble strategies were compared: the conventional Multi-Model Ensemble Mean (MME), in which climate variables are averaged before model simulation, and the Multi-Model Mean of Simulations (MMS), in which simulations are conducted separately for each climate model and subsequently averaged. Consequently, the MMS projections more closely approximate the mean trajectory of the individual CMIP6-driven simulations. The projections show relatively high reliability. title: The ecology and evolution of the model species Xenopus laevis
authors: Dareen Almojil; John Measey; Stéphane Boissinot
abstract: The African clawed frog Xenopus laevis has been a cornerstone of experimental biology for over a century, but its value as a model organism extends far beyond embryology. title: Reconstruction of China ecological fiscal transfer system from the perspective of fiscal verticality and horizontality
authors: Mengba Liu; Yanni Gu; Rongman Zhu; Shuling Jiao; Junjie Lin

title: Period-doubling bifurcation and harvesting control: prey-predator-scavenger system with additional food and fear effects
authors: Vinita Vinayak Gadgoli; Reenu Rani; Rajalakshmi Manoharan; Anuj Kumar

The article advances ecological grief science in five ways. First, it moves analysis beyond individual resilience, burnout, and communication failure by locating grief-like scientific distress within knowledge governance. Second, it connects ecological grief scholarship with Earth-system risk governance, including planetary boundaries, tipping points, cascading risk, resilience governance, and anticipatory governance. Third, it specifies a cross-level mechanism linking repeated ecological observation and actionability appraisal at the micro level, research-organizational and boundary mediation at the meso level, and governance mandates and authority structures at the macro level. Fourth, it converts the concept into propositions, boundary conditions, rival explanations, and observable indicators for empirical research. Fifth, it uses Sikkim in the Eastern Himalaya as an illustrative plausibility probe to show how evidence on alpine ecological change, spring decline and repair, hydropower contestation, Indigenous territorial authority, and South Lhonak glacial-lake hazard can accumulate while authority remains sectoral and fragmented.

title: Before they can name ecological grief: a brief research report of young children’s climate emotions in a small island state
authors: Jane Spiteri
abstract: Climate emotions research is expanding rapidly, yet children under eight remain less visible than adolescents and adults within the field despite evidence that climate concern may emerge early in life. Such an omission is especially consequential in small island states that are more vulnerable to climate change. This Brief Research Report presents a secondary qualitative analysis of empirical studies conducted in Malta with young children, parents and early childhood educators. Re-examining these datasets through the lens of climate emotions, the analysis shows that young children express early forms of climate worry and ecological loss through concrete, place-based concerns about heat, pollution, animals, the sea and damaged environments, even without adult terminology. Parents and educators recognise climate risks but often struggle to communicate them in emotionally safe ways. The findings conceptualise climate emotions in early childhood as an emergent, relational and co-constructed experience shaped by place attachment, intergenerational communication and opportunities for care-based action. The report further suggests that children’s climate emotions are socially mediated through family, educational and peer contexts. Finally, it argues that conservation social science must integrate young children’s emotional responses to ecological loss, particularly in small island contexts where the impacts of climate change are more pronounced and encountered intimately and daily.

title: Close encounters: responses of road users to wild chimpanzee road crossings in Uganda
authors: Marie Tellier; Marie Cibot; François Druelle; John-Mary Baruzaliire; Tom Sabiiti; Matthew R. McLennan
abstract: Expanding road networks increasingly encroach on wildlife home ranges, intensifying human-animal interactions. While ecological consequences like habitat fragmentation or wildlife mortality from vehicle collisions are well-studied, immediate behavioral responses of human road users during wildlife encounters remain underexplored despite their critical impact on safety and conservation. This study investigates behavioral responses of vulnerable (pedestrians, cyclists) and non-vulnerable (motorists) road users during wild chimpanzee ( Pan troglodytes ) crossings in a human-dominated landscape in Bulindi, Uganda. We analyzed 376 opportunistically recorded interactions over 38 months to identify factors influencing road users’ caution (stopping or slowing down without interfering with the chimpanzees, or retreating) and interest (stopping or slowing down to watch, including approaching chimpanzees). Local pedestrians and cyclists displayed significantly higher caution than motorists. Caution and interest did not differ significantly by age or sex among pedestrians. Road users were generally more cautious and curious when chimpanzees actively crossed the road compared to waiting at the roadside. Conversely, encounters with larger chimpanzee groups correlated with reduced caution. Interactions with local field assistants, employed to monitor the chimpanzees, increased both caution and interest among road users. Although no collisions occurred, seven near-miss incidents were documented, primarily linked to poor visibility and reckless motorcyclist behavior. These results show that road user behavior is influenced by physical vulnerability, chimpanzee visibility, and contextual cues, highlighting potential risk factors for both humans and chimpanzees. Despite chimpanzee adaptability to anthropogenic environmental change, roads and traffic remain significant threats to this endangered species. Our findings emphasize the need for measures to limit vehicle speed (e.g., speed humps, signs, traffic controls) and improve visibility on roads traversing chimpanzee habitats, coupled with targeted awareness campaigns for local communities, tourists, and non-resident workers, as well as the integration of locally based and trusted personnel into road safety strategies.

title: Geographic variation in behavioral avoidance of a widespread contaminant by Gulf killifish Fundulus grandis
authors: Charles W. Martin; Ashley M. McDonald; Kathryn A. O’Shaughnessy
abstract: Understanding the behavioral response of estuarine fishes to environmental contaminants is critical for assessing the ecological consequences of disturbances. Here, we examined geographic variation in avoidance behavior to petroleum-contaminated sediments in the Gulf killifish ( Fundulus grandis ), a sentinel species in northern Gulf of Mexico marshes. Adult fish were collected from four geographically distinct estuaries: Terrebonne Bay, Louisiana; Mississippi Sound, Alabama; Pensacola Bay, Florida; and Cedar Key, Florida. Choice experiments tested fish preference to either uncontaminated sediments or sediments contaminated with fresh or weathered oil. Results found significant differences among source locations with individuals from western Gulf sites (Louisiana and Alabama) exhibiting strong avoidance of fresh oil, while those from eastern sites (Florida) showed limited or no avoidance. No source location avoided weathered oil. These findings suggest that sensitivity to oil contamination varies regionally, potentially reflecting local exposure histories, environmental adaptation, or other sources of geographic variation. The diminished response to weathered oil across all locations highlights a reduced ability to detect residual contamination and indicates that these fish may use more volatile compounds that precipitate or degrade faster as a cue. This study underscores the importance of incorporating behavioral and geographic-level variability into impact assessments and emphasizes the need for regionally-tailored conservation strategies.
